analysis.one_liner: Broadens the federal bribery law so more favors to officials count as bribes.
analysis.headline: The anti-bribery bill died without a single hearing, never reaching a House floor vote in the two years before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court narrowed what counts as bribery in its McDonnell decision, this bill would have written a broader definition into federal law: a public official's 'personal and substantial participation' — advising, investigating, recommending, approving or disapproving a matter — could count as the 'official act' that makes a gift or payment a bribe. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it sat until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want public officials held accountable when they take things of value in exchange for using their position — the bill makes it easier to prosecute officials whose conduct falls into the gap left after McDonnell v. United States, where favor-pulling that falls short of a formal decision was held not to be bribery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking accountability for official favor-peddling

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the bribery statute so that an official's personal and substantial participation in a matter — for example, approving, disapproving, recommending, giving advice on, or investigating it — counts as an 'official act' that can make a thing of value exchanged for it a bribe.

The current definition covers only decisions or actions on questions that may come before a public official, which the Supreme Court's McDonnell decision interpreted to exclude less formal favors such as arranging meetings and urging subordinates to act; this bill would close that gap by statute.

analysis.who_pays: Public officials who accept things of value for pushing or advising on private interests' matters would face broader criminal exposure, as would the lobbyists, companies, and donors who pay for that influence — conduct that is now hard to charge would become chargeable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Officials and interests buying informal influence

drawbacks.text: The broadened language — 'personal and substantial participation' that includes 'rendering of advice' or even 'recommendation' — reaches well past formal decisions, and critics of expanding the bribery statute after McDonnell have warned that definitions this broad can sweep in routine constituent service and ordinary meetings between officials and citizens, chilling legitimate daily work in Congress and agencies.

Criminal law that is vague is also dangerous in practice: a definition stretched to cover advice and investigation could be enforced selectively against political opponents, and courts would have to spend years drawing the line the bill leaves blurry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Closing the McDonnell gap is a real accountability gain: favor-pulling for pay that no prosecutor can currently reach would become chargeable. The honest cost is that the bill's key phrase is broader than the problem — 'rendering of advice' and 'recommendation' could drag routine constituent casework into criminal territory. A narrower draft could have closed the loophole with less overreach, but as written it is a genuine, if blunt, strengthening of anti-corruption law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, so the bill died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Suozzi introduced the bill on September 26, 2017, joined at introduction by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, giving it one Democratic and one Republican sponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary; a week later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Republicans, and never grew beyond that.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public officials and the lobbyists, companies, and donors who trade on informal influence are better off, because the narrower post-McDonnell reading of the bribery statute — under which favors short of formal decisions are hard to charge — remains the law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials and lobbyists keeping the bribery loophole

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan and tiny: one Democratic sponsor, two Republican cosponsors, and no recorded opposition — it died from inaction, not a party vote.

industries.note: The bill would have expanded what counts as a bribe to include paid-for advice, recommendations, and steering — much of the informal influence business that grew safer after McDonnell. Its failure keeps that conduct outside the bribery statute.

industries.industry: Public officials (Members of Congress and agency heads)
industries.note: The bill's criminal exposure falls on officeholders who take things of value for personal and substantial participation in private matters. Its death preserves the narrower standard under which such conduct is hard to prosecute.
